newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE - TV casts long shadow over Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - TV casts long shadow over Indonesia.

text.p: The swift growth of satellite television across Indonesia and the nation's unlimited access to what is seen as a service spreading foreign values has worried many, including the government, in the multi-ethnic archipelago.

President Suharto has said he is concerned about the "tremendous threat" posed by the growth in global information flows and the impact of foreign ideas on Indonesia's 200 million population, composed of 300 ethnic groups and 583 languages and dialects.
Unlike neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore, Indonesia has no restrictions on satellite dish ownership.

The dishes that pick up tightly controlled state television and five local private channels received off Indonesia's Palapa satellites, can also access a host of regional and international broadcasters across the Moslem-majority nation's 17,000 islands.

"Indonesia has an open skies policy and it has created changes, as by putting dishes everywhere the people can look and learn about values, aspirations and experiences of people in other countries," said leading Islamic intellectual Adi Sasono.

"The free flow of global information has brought people in all countries closer. This enables people to receive foreign values that can erode their sense of nationalism," Suharto, 75, warned in a speech in early March.
"So extreme is the impact of foreign influences, some people no longer care about maintaining their nation's unity," he said.
GLOBAL FLOW OF INFORMATION UNSTOPPABLE
Sasono, secretary-general of Indonesia's Association of Islamic Intelltectuals (ICMI), said the global flow of information is unstoppable.
"Nobody can stop this process, it's irreversible," he said.

Analysts disagreed with Suharto's dire warnings, saying he is repeating a familiar line not supported by reality and that exposure to foreign media broadcasts did not necessarily encourage political dissent.

"Suharto dislikes the increased visibility for political dissent afforded by the greatly enhanced flow of information in and out of Indonesia," said John Macdougall, political analyst and editor of Indonesia Publications based in the Washington D.C. area.

"Separatist movements in Indonesia generally do not get substantial impetus from information globalisation," he said. "These movements mainly orginate and sustain themselves from events on the ground.
"Domestic dissidents tend to set the agendas for their foreign supporters, not the other way around," he added.

Krishna Sen, a fellow at the Asia Research Centre at Murdoch University in Perth, Australia said criticism of the government had risen as Indonesia's professional class developed and more people had the opportunity for overseas education and travel.

Also, "television is by far the most important source of information and entertainment...throughout Asia," Sen said. "There are villages in Central Java which have 60 television households and only two newspaper subscribers."
SATELLITE TV REACHES REMOTE VILLAGES
Indonesians in remote villages can tune in at all hours to programmes from foreign broadcasters like CNN, Australian Broadcasting Corp, neighbouring Malaysian television and others.
While proficiency in English is often patchy, visitors to the archipelago's remote islands are often surprised at the number of people who watch Western media broadcasts.
What worries Indonesian security and information officials is that information and images that never appear in the domestic media are available from international broadcasters.
Local media coverage of recent ethnic riots in West Kalimantan was suppressed, but satellite broadcasts showed potentially explosive images of whole burnt villages.
In East Timor, residents can watch broadcasts from Jakarta's arch diplomatic rival in Lisbon.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in an act not recognised by the United Nations, which still considers former colonial rule Portugal as the administering power.
UPCOMING ELECTIONS MAY HELP IN SPREAD
A decision by authorities to take the campaign for next month's general elections onto television screens is an acknowledgement of the power of the medium, analysts say.

The government says it wants to raise the quality of the campaign by airing tightly controlled televised debates rather than letting parties hold outdoor rallies, which in the past have sometimes been unruly.

"If television is involved in the campaign, people will soon be tempted to demand a further extension of satellite television services," Indonesian political analyst Ariel Heryanto wrote in a recent column in the leading Kompas daily.
